items.prompt: Meridian and Castellan were breached through the identical 0-day, on identically-patched web servers. Why did only Meridian have to notify 14 million customers?
choices: Meridian's 0-day was more severe than Castellan's

Castellan's architecture limited what a compromised web server could reach — segmented network, a DB account scoped to 2 tables — while Meridian's flat-trust design let the same foothold reach the whole database
Castellan simply patched faster
Meridian didn't have a firewall at all
items.explanation: The vulnerability itself was identical — same library, same 0-day, same weekend. What differed was a design decision made months earlier: Castellan's web server held a database credential scoped to SELECT on 2 tables, behind a network segment that didn't even route to the database directly, so the attacker's code execution had nowhere useful to go. Meridian's web server held full admin DB credentials with a direct network path, so the same foothold reached everything.
items.reference:
Meridian

admin creds, direct route → 14M records

Castellan

scoped creds, segmented route → 2 tables

Why: the breach was identical; the architecture decided the outcome.

items.prompt: If you wanted to explain, in one sentence, why the SAME vulnerability produced two different outcomes at Meridian and Castellan, which explanation is correct?
choices: The outcome was decided at breach time by how skilled each attacker was
The outcome was decided beforehand, by what each system assumed would happen once one component failed
The outcome depended only on which company had cyber insurance
The outcome depended on which company discovered the breach first
items.explanation: Both attackers used the same exploit against the same class of foothold — the skill required was identical. What differed was a design-time decision: whether the architecture assumed a compromised component might happen (Castellan) and bounded what it could reach, or assumed the perimeter defenses would simply hold (Meridian) and never bounded anything past that point.
items.reference:
Meridian

admin creds, direct route → 14M records

Castellan

scoped creds, segmented route → 2 tables

Why: the breach was identical; the architecture decided the outcome.

items.prompt: Castellan's web server, after the breach, still had code execution — the attacker fully controlled it. Why couldn't the attacker just read the database directly from there?
choices: Because the database itself was encrypted end-to-end so no query could work
Because there was no network route from the web tier to the database, and the credentials available on the web server could only read 2 non-sensitive tables even where a route existed
Because the attacker's exploit only worked on Mondays
Because Castellan's web server was air-gapped and had no internet access at all
items.explanation: Code execution on the web server gives an attacker whatever that server itself can reach and whatever credentials it holds — nothing more automatically. Castellan's design meant that server had no network path to the database at all except through a proxy, and even the credential it did hold for that proxy was scoped to SELECT on 2 tables. Full control of a component isn't the same as full control of everything that component might theoretically be near.
items.reference:
Meridian

admin creds, direct route → 14M records

Castellan

scoped creds, segmented route → 2 tables

Why: the breach was identical; the architecture decided the outcome.

items.prompt: Which best describes "defense in depth" as this unit uses the term?
choices: Buying the single strongest security product available and relying on it exclusively
Multiple independent, layered controls, each one designed assuming the layer before it has already failed
Running the same virus scanner on every server for consistency
Encrypting data twice with two different algorithms
items.explanation: Defense in depth isn't about having one very strong control, or many copies of the same control — it's about stacking controls that each check something genuinely different, so a single failure anywhere in the stack doesn't automatically mean total compromise. Network segmentation, scoped credentials, and per-request authorization each stop a different category of attacker action.
items.reference:
network segmentation → WAF → authn → authz → scoped credential → encryption → monitoring — each layer assumes the one before it already failed

Why: depth means independence, not redundancy.

items.prompt: A team adds a second firewall product from a different vendor, in front of their existing one, both configured to block the same categories of malicious traffic. Is this a good example of defense in depth?
choices: Yes — two firewalls is always better than one, regardless of what they check

Not really — both are answering the same question about the same category of traffic, so anything that evades one has a real chance of evading the other too; true depth comes from layers that check genuinely different things
No, because firewalls from different vendors can never work together
Yes, because more vendors always means more security budget was spent
items.explanation: Two firewalls scanning for the same kind of malicious traffic are closer to redundancy than depth — they raise the cost of getting past that one specific checkpoint, but they don't give an attacker a fundamentally different kind of problem to solve. A genuinely independent layer — like a least-privilege credential that limits what's reachable even after the network is bypassed entirely — checks something the firewall never could.
items.reference:
network segmentation → WAF → authn → authz → scoped credential → encryption → monitoring — each layer assumes the one before it already failed

Why: depth means independence, not redundancy.

items.prompt: What's the key assumption each layer in a defense-in-depth stack is built on?
choices: That every layer above it in the stack will always hold, so its own check rarely matters
That the layer before it has already failed, so it must be able to stop the attacker on its own, independently
That attackers only ever target the first layer in the stack
That all layers should use the exact same detection technique for consistency
items.explanation: A layer that assumes everything upstream already held isn't really a layer — it's decoration. Real defense in depth designs each control as if it were the only one left standing: network segmentation as if the WAF already failed, a scoped credential as if authorization already failed, monitoring as if every preventive control already failed.
items.reference:
network segmentation → WAF → authn → authz → scoped credential → encryption → monitoring — each layer assumes the one before it already failed

Why: depth means independence, not redundancy.

items.prompt: What question does the principle of least privilege actually try to answer?
choices: "Is this account convenient to maintain?"
"If this exact credential is stolen or misused right now, what's the smallest possible set of things that can go wrong?"
"How many people should know this password?"
"Is this the cheapest possible access-control system to build?"
items.explanation: Least privilege is fundamentally about bounding the blast radius of a single compromised credential — scoping every account, service, and process down to exactly what it needs, so that when (not if) something is stolen or misused, the damage is contained to that scope rather than the whole system.
items.reference:
shared admin account → all 47 tables exposed vs. scoped read account → 2 tables exposed, same theft

Why: least privilege bounds the damage a stolen credential can do.

items.prompt: "Just give the service admin access, it's simpler to maintain" is a common justification for over-provisioning a service account. What does this unit say is actually wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Nothing — admin access is always fine as long as the password is strong
It optimizes for convenience today at the cost of blast radius later — it's the path of least effort, which is the opposite of least privilege
It's wrong because admin accounts are always slower than scoped ones
It's wrong only if the company has fewer than 100 employees
items.explanation: Scoping access down is real, ongoing work — someone has to determine exactly what a service needs and keep that current. "Just use admin" avoids that work, which is exactly why it's tempting and exactly why it's the opposite of least privilege: it trades a bounded blast radius later for convenience now.
items.reference:
shared admin account → all 47 tables exposed vs. scoped read account → 2 tables exposed, same theft

Why: least privilege bounds the damage a stolen credential can do.

items.prompt: What does "zero trust" mean, as this unit uses the phrase?
choices: No system should ever trust any user, so login should be disabled entirely
Being on the internal network, or behind the firewall, grants no default trust — every request is verified on its own merits, regardless of where it came from
Trusting zero vendors and building every security tool in-house
A policy of never granting access to anyone, ever
items.explanation: Zero trust is specifically about removing network location as an implicit trust signal. A request from "inside the firewall" or from another internal service gets no free pass — it's authenticated and authorized the same way an external request would be, every time.
items.reference:
perimeter-only: inside the firewall = trusted, no re-check vs. zero trust: every call re-verified, including internal ones

Why: network location was never proof of identity or permission.

items.prompt: A "perimeter-only" (castle-and-moat) architecture puts its serious checks where?
choices: At every single internal service boundary, equally, with no special treatment for the edge
At the network edge — firewall, VPN, login — after which everything "inside" is treated as roughly trusted
Nowhere — perimeter-only architectures have no checks at all
Only inside the database layer
items.explanation: Perimeter-only security concentrates verification at the boundary and assumes anything that made it past that boundary can be trusted from then on. That's exactly the assumption zero trust rejects — it treats every call, internal or external, as needing its own verification.
items.reference:
perimeter-only: inside the firewall = trusted, no re-check vs. zero trust: every call re-verified, including internal ones

Why: network location was never proof of identity or permission.

items.prompt: Why does Meridian's breach specifically illustrate a failure of zero trust, and not just a failure of "having no security"?
choices: It doesn't — Meridian had literally no security controls anywhere

Meridian likely had a firewall and login page too, but once the attacker's foothold was "inside" that perimeter, nothing re-verified it before it reached the database — exactly the gap zero trust closes
Because Meridian used the wrong brand of firewall
Because zero trust only applies to companies with more than 1,000 employees
items.explanation: Meridian almost certainly had perimeter defenses. What it lacked was any checkpoint inside that perimeter — once the web server was compromised, it was itself "inside," and nothing asked it to re-prove anything before talking to the database. That's precisely the assumption zero trust removes.
items.reference:
perimeter-only: inside the firewall = trusted, no re-check vs. zero trust: every call re-verified, including internal ones

Why: network location was never proof of identity or permission.

items.prompt: `authorization-models` covers RBAC/ABAC — deciding whether one specific request is allowed right now. How is this unit's territory different?
choices: It isn't different — this unit just repeats authorization models with different examples
This unit assumes authorization already exists and asks: if it fails, or a component is bypassed entirely, what stops one failure from becoming total compromise?
This unit replaces authorization models entirely — you no longer need RBAC/ABAC if you have defense in depth
This unit is only about network hardware, not access control at all
items.explanation: Authorization models are about getting one check right at request time. This unit starts from the premise that any single check — authentication, authorization, or something else entirely like a 0-day — can eventually fail, and asks what architectural decisions bound the damage when that happens, rather than how to make any one check more correct.
items.reference:
authorization-models: is THIS request allowed? vs. defense-depth: if a component is breached, what can it reach?

Why: this unit assumes a check has already failed somewhere.

items.prompt: `owasp-top-10` surveys individual vulnerability categories (injection, broken access control, etc). Why doesn't this unit just duplicate that survey?
choices: Because this unit covers a completely disjoint set of vulnerabilities that OWASP doesn't mention
Because this unit isn't about which specific bug let an attacker in — it's about what happens architecturally regardless of which bug it was
Because OWASP Top 10 and defense in depth are actually the same thing under different names
Because this unit only applies to vulnerabilities discovered before 2020
items.explanation: OWASP Top 10 answers "what's the specific flaw that let this happen" — injection, broken access control, and so on. This unit deliberately doesn't care which specific flaw it was; a 0-day, a stolen credential, and a malicious dependency all end up asking the same architectural question: once a component is compromised by whatever means, what can it reach?
items.reference:
authorization-models: is THIS request allowed? vs. defense-depth: if a component is breached, what can it reach?

Why: this unit assumes a check has already failed somewhere.

items.prompt: A company runs two WAFs from different vendors in front of each other, both scanning for the same categories of attack payloads. Is this genuine defense in depth?
choices: Yes — any additional product automatically counts as another layer

Not really — both check the same category of input for the same kind of pattern, so whatever evades the first has a real chance of evading the second too; a genuine second layer asks a different question entirely
No, because running two WAFs is technically impossible
Yes, but only if both vendors are headquartered in different countries
items.explanation: Layering only helps when each control checks something the others don't. Two WAFs scanning the same payload category for the same attack patterns are closer to redundancy — a least-privilege credential scoped to specific tables asks a fundamentally different question ("can this credential even do this") that stays effective even against payloads no WAF ever recognized as malicious.
items.reference:
2 WAFs, same signature class = redundancy vs. WAF + scoped credential = independent questions

Why: a layer earns its place by checking something no other layer checks.

items.prompt: Castellan's scoped DB account stopped an attacker who had ALREADY defeated network segmentation, authentication, and authorization (they had real code execution, not a forged request). What made that layer effective even after everything upstream had failed?
choices: It re-ran the same authentication check a second time
It asked a completely different question — "can this specific credential even do this" — independent of who or what was holding it, so bypassing the upstream layers didn't help defeat it too
It was simply a stronger version of the network segmentation layer
It relied on the attacker not knowing SQL
items.explanation: Genuine layers don't share a common weakness. The scoped credential layer doesn't care how the caller got there or what identity it's claiming — it only asks whether the credential in hand is permitted to do the specific operation requested, a question upstream layers never answered and couldn't help an attacker answer either.
items.reference:
2 WAFs, same signature class = redundancy vs. WAF + scoped credential = independent questions

Why: a layer earns its place by checking something no other layer checks.

items.prompt: Which of these pairs is an example of genuinely INDEPENDENT layers, in the sense this unit means?
choices: Two intrusion-detection systems both scanning network traffic for the same known attack signatures
Network segmentation ("can this component even reach the DB tier?") and least-privilege scoping ("can this credential even do this operation?")
Running the same password-strength check on both the login form and the password-reset form
Two firewalls with identical rule sets, one behind the other
items.explanation: Network segmentation and credential scoping fail independently of each other: segmentation is defeated by having a network path, scoping is defeated by an over-broad grant — an attacker has to beat both separately, because success against one doesn't imply anything about the other. The other options are variations on checking the same thing twice.
items.reference:
2 WAFs, same signature class = redundancy vs. WAF + scoped credential = independent questions

Why: a layer earns its place by checking something no other layer checks.

items.prompt: Meridian's web server holds a shared admin account with access to all 47 tables. Castellan's holds a scoped account with SELECT on 2 tables. If BOTH credentials are stolen via an identical technique, what determines the difference in outcome?
choices: Nothing — a stolen credential always exposes the entire database regardless of scope
What was granted to each credential BEFORE the theft — the theft technique is identical, but the account's own scope decides what the thief can do with it
Only the strength of each account's password
Whether the company has cyber insurance
items.explanation: A stolen credential can only do what it was ever granted — theft doesn't expand scope, it just hands the thief whatever scope already existed. That's why the grant decision, made before any breach, is the thing that actually determines the outcome once one happens.
items.reference:
shared admin: 47 tables, all ops vs. scoped reader: 2 tables, SELECT only — same theft technique, different blast radius

Why: a stolen credential can only do what it was already granted.

items.prompt: Why is least-privilege scoping described as "ongoing work" rather than a one-time setting?
choices: Because passwords need to be rotated every 90 days regardless of scope
Because a service's actual needs change as the app changes, so the minimal-necessary scope has to be re-derived over time, not set once and forgotten
Because database vendors require re-scoping as a licensing condition
It isn't ongoing work — once scoped correctly, it never needs revisiting
items.explanation: "Minimum necessary access" is only accurate at the moment it's defined — as features are added or removed, what a service actually needs shifts, and a grant that was minimal a year ago can silently become over-broad if nobody revisits it. Least privilege has to be maintained, not just configured once.
items.reference:
shared admin: 47 tables, all ops vs. scoped reader: 2 tables, SELECT only — same theft technique, different blast radius

Why: a stolen credential can only do what it was already granted.

items.prompt: A team under deadline pressure widens a service account's scope "just for now" to unblock a feature, planning to narrow it back later. What does this unit's framing say about that decision?
choices: It's fine, since scope can always be narrowed instantly whenever anyone remembers to do it
It's the same failure pattern as hardcoding a secret under deadline pressure — a temporary convenience that quietly becomes the system's actual blast radius until someone deliberately revisits it
It's required, since databases don't allow scope changes after initial setup
It has no security implication as long as the widened scope is documented somewhere
items.explanation: Widening scope "temporarily" under pressure is exactly the kind of decision that tends to outlive the deadline that justified it — nothing forces it back down automatically. Until it's deliberately re-scoped, the system's actual blast radius is whatever was granted under pressure, not whatever was originally intended.
items.reference:
shared admin: 47 tables, all ops vs. scoped reader: 2 tables, SELECT only — same theft technique, different blast radius

Why: a stolen credential can only do what it was already granted.

items.prompt: In a perimeter-only architecture, once service A is "inside" and calls service B, what typically happens?
choices: Service B re-authenticates and re-authorizes the call from scratch, exactly as if it came from outside
Service B implicitly trusts the call because it came from inside the same network, with no independent re-check
The call is blocked by default unless explicitly allowed, the same as an external call
Service B routes the call back out through the firewall for inspection first
items.explanation: That implicit trust — "it's inside, so it must be fine" — is exactly what perimeter-only architectures grant and zero trust removes. Once a request is inside the perimeter, nothing independently re-verifies it, which is precisely the gap a compromised internal component can exploit.
items.reference:
perimeter-only: A calls B, implicitly trusted vs. zero trust: A calls B, mTLS + per-request authz, every time

Why: "inside the network" was never proof of anything on its own.

items.prompt: Under zero trust, a service-to-service call entirely inside the same cluster still gets mutual TLS and a per-request authorization check. What's the actual justification for this, given that call never left the internal network?
choices: It's pure redundancy with no real justification — internal calls are inherently safe

The threat model isn't an external attacker reaching a private IP — it's a component already inside that perimeter, compromised through some other route, for which "internal network" no longer distinguishes attacker from legitimate service
Mutual TLS is required by law for all internal traffic
It's only needed if the cluster spans multiple cloud providers
items.explanation: Once the premise is "one component might already be compromised," being on the internal network describes the compromised component's position just as accurately as a legitimate service's — the IP range alone can't tell them apart. Per-request mTLS and authorization verify the caller's actual identity and permissions, a property network location never established.
items.reference:
perimeter-only: A calls B, implicitly trusted vs. zero trust: A calls B, mTLS + per-request authz, every time

Why: "inside the network" was never proof of anything on its own.

items.prompt: What's the single biggest structural difference between a perimeter-only architecture and a zero-trust one?
choices: Zero trust has no firewall at all, while perimeter-only relies entirely on one
Perimeter-only concentrates its real checks at the network edge; zero trust re-verifies every request, including internal ones, regardless of where it originated
Zero trust is only usable for companies with fewer than 10 services
Perimeter-only encrypts data at rest while zero trust does not
items.explanation: The structural shift is where verification happens: perimeter-only puts nearly all of it at the edge and trusts what's already inside; zero trust distributes verification to every request, treating "already inside" as carrying no special trust at all.
items.reference:
perimeter-only: A calls B, implicitly trusted vs. zero trust: A calls B, mTLS + per-request authz, every time

Why: "inside the network" was never proof of anything on its own.

items.prompt: A `NetworkPolicy` allows service A to reach service B. Under zero trust, does that mean service B should skip authenticating and authorizing A's specific request?
choices: Yes — if the network allows the connection, that's sufficient proof of trust
No — the network policy only controls whether a packet can arrive at all; it says nothing about who's actually sending it or what they're allowed to ask for, which is a separate check
Yes, but only for read-only requests
No, but only because Kubernetes NetworkPolicies are unreliable
items.explanation: A network policy answers a routing question — can this packet reach that destination — not an identity or permission question. Whether the specific caller is who it claims to be, and whether that identity is allowed to do the specific thing it's asking for, are separate checks that have to happen regardless of what the network already allowed.
items.reference:
NetworkPolicy: can the packet arrive? vs. mTLS + authz: who sent it, and are they allowed to ask for this?

Why: network reachability and per-request authorization are two different questions.

items.prompt: In a service-to-service mTLS check, why is the caller's identity read from a verified client certificate's Subject CN, rather than from a header like `X-Service-Name` the caller sends itself?
choices: Headers are always slower to parse than certificates
A header is just a claim the caller could set to anything; a cert CN validated against a trusted CA is a verified fact the caller can't forge without also compromising the CA
There's no real difference — either one works equally well
Certificates are required by GDPR for all internal traffic
items.explanation: Anything the caller sends as plain data — a header, a body field — can be set to whatever the caller wants, including by a compromised component impersonating someone else. A certificate that chains to a CA the receiver already trusts is verified independently of what the caller claims about itself, which is what makes it usable for actual identity, not just a label.
items.reference:
NetworkPolicy: can the packet arrive? vs. mTLS + authz: who sent it, and are they allowed to ask for this?

Why: network reachability and per-request authorization are two different questions.

items.prompt: Which question does the LEAST-PRIVILEGE layer specifically ask, that the AUTHORIZATION layer doesn't?
choices: "Is this request coming from a logged-in user?"
"Even if this identity is authorized for this action, does the underlying credential it's using actually have the technical permission to do it?"
"Is the network connection encrypted?"
"Has this user's password been rotated recently?"
items.explanation: Authorization checks whether an identity is allowed to perform an action according to policy. Least-privilege scoping is a separate, lower-level backstop: even if authorization says yes, the actual database/service credential being used to perform the action might not technically be able to — a second, independent gate on the same action.
items.reference:
network: can it route there? · authz: is this identity allowed? · least privilege: can the credential itself even do it?

Why: each layer answers a distinct question about the same request.

items.prompt: Which question does NETWORK SEGMENTATION ask, that no credential-scoping layer can answer on its own?
choices: "Is this credential's password long enough?"
"Can this component even reach that destination at the network level, regardless of what credentials it might be holding?"
"Is the caller's identity cryptographically verified?"
"Has this data been encrypted at rest?"
items.explanation: Network segmentation operates a level below credentials entirely — it decides whether a connection can be established at all. A perfectly-scoped credential is irrelevant if there's no network path to use it over, which is exactly why Castellan's segmentation stopped the attacker even before the scoped account came into play.
items.reference:
network: can it route there? · authz: is this identity allowed? · least privilege: can the credential itself even do it?

Why: each layer answers a distinct question about the same request.

items.prompt: Implement `canAccess(grants, role, table, operation)`. `grants` is shaped like `{ web_catalog_reader: { products: ['SELECT'], product_categories: ['SELECT'] } }` — mirroring the explicit SQL GRANTs from the deep dive. Return `true` only if `role` exists in `grants`, `table` is granted to that role, AND `operation` is in that table's allowed operations list. Anything not explicitly granted (an unknown role, an unlisted table, or an operation not in the list) must return `false` — the same default-deny posture as the SQL `REVOKE`s.

tests.description: granted role/table/operation returns true
table not granted to this role returns false
operation not in the granted list returns false
unknown role returns false, not a crash

items.explanation: This is the SQL GRANT/REVOKE table from L3 read back as code: every lookup that isn't explicitly present in `grants` short-circuits to `false`, matching PostgreSQL's own default-deny behavior where anything not GRANTed stays inaccessible. There's no implicit fallback to 'probably fine' anywhere in the chain — a missing role, a missing table, or an operation absent from the list all deny identically.
items.reference:
GRANT SELECT ON products TO web_catalog_reader; everything not explicitly GRANTed stays denied by default

Why: a stolen credential can only do what was explicitly granted to it.

items.prompt: Implement `canAccess(grants, role, table, operation)` for a different service account. `grants` looks like `{ order_processing_writer: { orders: ['SELECT', 'INSERT', 'UPDATE'], products: ['SELECT'] } }`. Return `true` only if the role, table, and operation are all explicitly present in the grant; otherwise `false`.

tests.description: granted write operation returns true
operation never granted for this table returns false
role has no grant at all for a sensitive table

items.explanation: order-processing-service legitimately needs to write orders (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE), which is exactly why over-broad grants are tempting: a real, working service needs real write access somewhere. The scoping discipline is granting exactly that (orders, three operations) and nothing beyond it — DELETE was never asked for, so it's never granted, and payment_methods was never part of this role's job.
items.reference:
GRANT SELECT ON products TO web_catalog_reader; everything not explicitly GRANTed stays denied by default

Why: a stolen credential can only do what was explicitly granted to it.

items.prompt: Implement `canAccess(grants, role, table, operation)` for a billing service account. `grants` looks like `{ billing_reader: { payment_methods: ['SELECT'], orders: ['SELECT'] } }`. Same rule as before: only an explicit role/table/operation match returns `true`.

tests.description: explicit read grant returns true
write operation was never granted, even on a table the role can read
a completely unrelated table returns false

items.explanation: billing_reader can read payment_methods, which is sensitive data, but read-only — it was never granted UPDATE/DELETE, and it has no grant at all for admin_audit_log. This is the same scoping logic as the other variants, applied to a role whose job genuinely does touch sensitive data; least privilege doesn't mean 'never touch sensitive tables,' it means 'touch exactly what's needed, no more.'
items.reference:
GRANT SELECT ON products TO web_catalog_reader; everything not explicitly GRANTed stays denied by default

Why: a stolen credential can only do what was explicitly granted to it.

items.prompt: Implement `isTrafficAllowed(policies, sourceTier, destTier, port)`, modeling the default-deny Kubernetes NetworkPolicies from the deep dive. `policies` is an array of `{ from, to, port }` objects — the ONLY explicitly allowed routes. Return `true` only if some policy entry exactly matches `sourceTier`, `destTier`, and `port`; otherwise `false` (default-deny, same as `default-deny-all.yaml`).

tests.description: web tier to db-proxy on the allowed port is allowed
web tier attempting to reach the database directly is denied (no such policy)
correct tiers but wrong port is denied

items.explanation: This mirrors default-deny-all.yaml plus the explicit web-tier-egress.yaml/db-tier-ingress.yaml policies: nothing is allowed unless it exactly matches an explicit entry. There's no partial-match or 'close enough' logic — the web tier having a valid route to db-proxy says nothing about whether it also has one to database, because that's a separate, unlisted route.
items.reference:
default-deny-all, then explicit egress/ingress rules per tier — nothing routes unless explicitly allowed

Why: scoped credentials are useless without a network path to use them over.

items.prompt: Implement `isTrafficAllowed(policies, sourceTier, destTier, port)` for a different set of tiers: `frontend` may reach `api-gateway` on port 443, and `api-gateway` may reach `database` on port 5432 — `frontend` has no direct policy to `database` at all. Same rule: return `true` only on an exact `{from, to, port}` match.

tests.description: api-gateway to database on the allowed port is allowed
tests.expr: expect(isTrafficAllowed([{ from: 'frontend', to: 'api-gateway', port: 443 }, { from: 'api-gateway', to: 'database', port: 5432 }], 'api-gateway', 'database', 5432)).toBe(true)

tests.description: frontend attempting to skip straight to database is denied
tests.expr: expect(isTrafficAllowed([{ from: 'frontend', to: 'api-gateway', port: 443 }, { from: 'api-gateway', to: 'database', port: 5432 }], 'frontend', 'database', 5432)).toBe(false)

tests.description: unrelated source tier is denied

items.explanation: Even though there's a legitimate multi-hop path from frontend to database (through api-gateway), that doesn't create an implicit direct route — frontend attempting to skip the gateway entirely has no matching policy and is denied, exactly like Castellan's web tier having no route directly to its database despite a valid path existing through the proxy.
items.reference:
default-deny-all, then explicit egress/ingress rules per tier — nothing routes unless explicitly allowed

Why: scoped credentials are useless without a network path to use them over.

items.prompt: Implement `isTrafficAllowed(policies, sourceTier, destTier, port)` where `worker` may reach `queue` on port 5672, and separately `queue` may reach `worker` on port 5673 (a reply channel) — these are two DIFFERENT one-directional policies, not automatically bidirectional. Return `true` only on an exact match.

tests.description: worker to queue on its allowed port is allowed
tests.expr: expect(isTrafficAllowed([{ from: 'worker', to: 'queue', port: 5672 }, { from: 'queue', to: 'worker', port: 5673 }], 'worker', 'queue', 5672)).toBe(true)

tests.description: worker to queue on the REPLY port (belongs to the other direction) is denied
tests.expr: expect(isTrafficAllowed([{ from: 'worker', to: 'queue', port: 5672 }, { from: 'queue', to: 'worker', port: 5673 }], 'worker', 'queue', 5673)).toBe(false)

tests.description: queue to worker on its own allowed port is allowed

items.explanation: A policy allowing worker to reach queue says nothing about queue reaching worker, or about a different port in either direction — each `{from, to, port}` combination is its own independent grant, matching how Kubernetes NetworkPolicy ingress and egress rules are genuinely separate and directional, never implicitly bidirectional.

items.prompt: Implement `authorize(permissions, caller, table, operation)`, modeling the zero-trust per-request check from the deep dive. `permissions` looks like `{ 'web-catalog-service': { products: ['SELECT'] } }`. Return `true` only if `caller` is a KNOWN key in `permissions` AND the table/operation is explicitly granted to it. A caller not present in `permissions` at all must return `false` just like an unlisted table would — the same default-deny posture whether the gap is at the caller level or the table level.

tests.description: known caller with an explicit grant is authorized
known caller asking for an ungranted table is denied
a caller with no entry in permissions at all is denied, not treated as an error

items.explanation: This is `authorizeQuery` from the deep dive, stripped down to a plain boolean return for testability. A caller with a valid mTLS certificate but no entry in `permissions` still gets denied — having a verified identity (WHO is calling, mTLS's job) is entirely separate from being authorized for a specific action (WHAT they're allowed to do, this function's job). Neither substitutes for the other.
items.reference:
mTLS proves WHO is calling · authorize() checks WHAT they're allowed to do — re-checked on every request, regardless of network origin

Why: zero trust means no upstream layer gets to substitute for this check.

items.prompt: Implement `blastRadius(graph, compromisedComponent)`, matching the deep dive's calculator. `graph` maps a component name to an array of `{ resource, recordCount, sensitivity }` grants. tests.description: Meridian-style: one broad grant sums to its full record count
tests.expr: expect(blastRadius({ 'web-server': [{ resource: 'all_tables', recordCount: 14000000, sensitivity: 'restricted' }] }, 'web-server')).toEqual({ totalRecordsExposed: 14000000, resourcesReached: [{ resource: 'all_tables', recordCount: 14000000, sensitivity: 'restricted' }] })

tests.expr: expect(blastRadius({ 'web-server': [{ resource: 'products', recordCount: 8200, sensitivity: 'public' }, { resource: 'product_categories', recordCount: 340, sensitivity: 'public' }] }, 'web-server').totalRecordsExposed).toBe(8540)

a component not present in the graph is treated as zero exposure, not a crash
tests.expr: expect(blastRadius({ 'web-server': [{ resource: 'x', recordCount: 5, sensitivity: 'public' }] }, 'unrelated-service')).toEqual({ totalRecordsExposed: 0, resourcesReached: [] })

Reusing the existing grant data as the source of truth is the point: this isn't a separate audit process to keep in sync, it's a different view of the same data.

tests.description: only the compromised component's own grants are counted
tests.expr: expect(blastRadius({ 'web-server': [{ resource: 'products', recordCount: 8200, sensitivity: 'public' }], 'billing-service': [{ resource: 'payment_methods', recordCount: 50000, sensitivity: 'restricted' }] }, 'web-server').totalRecordsExposed).toBe(8200)

items.explanation: web-server's compromise never pulls in billing-service's 50,000-record payment_methods exposure, and vice versa — each component's blast radius is computed strictly from its own direct grants. This single-hop scoping is exactly what the accompanying Checkpoint calls out as a real limitation: it doesn't account for one compromised component then pivoting to call another one, which needs a graph traversal, not a single lookup.

items.prompt: Implement `reachableComponents(adjacency, start)` — the lateral-movement extension the deep dive's Checkpoint describes. `adjacency` maps a component to the array of other components it can legitimately call, e.g. `{ 'order-processing': ['billing-reconciliation'], 'billing-reconciliation': ['database'] }`. Return an array of every component reachable from `start` via one or more hops (breadth-first, first-discovered order), NOT including `start` itself, with no duplicates even if there's a cycle back to an already-visited component.

tests.description: a 2-hop chain returns both downstream components in discovery order
a component with no outgoing calls reaches nothing
a cycle (a -> b -> c -> a) does not infinite-loop and does not duplicate entries

items.explanation: This is precisely the gap the accompanying Checkpoint names: `blastRadius()` only measures one component's direct grants, but a real attacker who compromises order-processing-service might pivot through it to reach billing-reconciliation-service, then database, none of which are direct grants of the original compromised component. BFS with a visited set both finds every multi-hop path and guarantees termination even when the call graph has cycles (a real risk in service meshes with bidirectional or circular call patterns).
items.reference:
order-processing → billing-reconciliation → database — blastRadius() alone misses this chain

Why: zero trust's per-hop re-authorization is what actually stops this chain, not measurement alone.
